**Video:** [Tutorial 10 Part A](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTEPAiwv-00)

## Learning goals

- Recover the **OLS** normal equations from matrix ERM with squared loss.
- Build a **Bayes classifier** from class-conditionals, priors, and losses.
- See how unequal misclassification costs shift the decision in an **overlap** region.

## Before this clicks

Bayes classifier (0–1 loss, equal priors): pick the class with larger posterior $P(Y=i\mid x)$, equivalently larger class-conditional times prior. With general losses, compare expected losses, not just posteriors. OLS: linear $h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x$ under squared ERM.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. OLS in matrix form (augmented features)

Stack $n$ examples into $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times (d+1)}$ (extra column of ones for bias) and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. ERM with squared loss:

$$
\theta^\star=\arg\min_\theta\frac{1}{n}\,\|X\theta-y\|_2^{2}.
$$

Expanding and setting the gradient to zero recovers the normal equations

$$
X^\top X\,\theta^\star = X^\top y
$$

(when $X^\top X$ is invertible, $\theta^\star=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$). Same optimum as the earlier per-example sum form.

### 2. Two-class Bayes setup (tutorial problem spirit)

Suppose $Y\in\{1,2\}$ with known (or given) class-conditionals on a feature $X$ (often uniform / piecewise densities on intervals in the board work), and priors $P(Y=1),P(Y=2)$.

Under **0–1 loss** with equal priors, Bayes compares $p(x\mid Y=i)$ (or posteriors). Decision regions:

- In the exclusive support of class $1$: predict $1$.
- Exclusive support of class $2$: predict $2$.
- In the **overlap** $S_{12}$: compare weighted conditionals.

### 3. Unequal costs move the overlap decision

If falsely predicting class $1$ is much more expensive (tutorial used a large cost factor, e.g. order $10$), the Bayes rule in the overlap can flip to the safer class even when raw densities look comparable.

Schematic comparison (equal priors): predict class $1$ only if

$$
\frac{p(x\mid Y=1)}{p(x\mid Y=2)}
>
\text{(cost-adjusted threshold)}.
$$

In the worked board calculation, the likelihood ratio in the overlap fell **below** the cost-adjusted threshold, so the entire overlap was assigned to class $2$.

### 4. Uniqueness

Bayes decision regions need not be unique if ties occur on sets of measure zero / equal risk alternatives. Different representations of the same partition can look different as formulas (e.g. a linear rule vs a set description) while agreeing almost everywhere — or disagree if the candidate rule is simply **not** Bayes.

---

## Worked mini-example

Equal priors, 0–1 loss. Supports: class 1 on $[0,4]$, class 2 on $[2,6]$, both uniform on their supports. Overlap $[2,4]$.

Density heights: $p(x\mid 1)=1/4$ on $[0,4]$, $p(x\mid 2)=1/4$ on $[2,6]$.

Equal costs $\Rightarrow$ either class is fine on a measure-zero knife-edge; with a **higher cost** for calling “1” when truth is “2”, prefer class $2$ throughout the overlap. Final Bayes-style rule:

- $[0,2)$: class $1$
- $[2,6]$: class $2$

(Exact constants in the video follow the problem sheet densities; the logic is identical.)

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| OLS formula needs centering always | Augment with a bias column instead (tutorial’s “augmented data”). |
| Bayes = compare densities only | Only after priors and losses are plugged in; costs change the threshold. |
| Any linear separator is Bayes | Must verify risk / posterior comparison; a hand-drawn line can fail in the overlap. |

2. Under 0–1 loss and equal priors, what does Bayes compare?
3. How do unequal misclassification costs affect the overlap region?
4. Why might two different-looking “Bayes classifiers” both be valid?
5. What does feature augmentation (column of ones) buy you?
